title: Fold steps into one Function with andThen and with compose

blocks.text: `f.andThen(g)` runs `f` first and then `g`: it is `g(f(x))`. `f.compose(g)` runs `g` first and then `f`: it is `f(g(x))`. Mixing the two up is a classic trap.
Write two methods in `Pipeline`. Each folds a list of `UnaryOperator<T>` steps into one `Function<T, T>`:

items: `inOrder(steps)` runs the steps first to last (`andThen` is the natural tool).
`inReverse(steps)` runs them last to first (`compose` is the natural tool).

blocks.text: A list may be empty. A step may return `null`; the step after it must not be handed that `null`, and the result is `null`. Any exception a step throws, a `NullPointerException` included, reaches the caller unchanged. The function is fixed when it is built: changing the list afterwards does not change it.

cases.says: inOrder runs the first step first; inReverse runs the last step first.
With no steps, both functions hand back their input itself.
When a step returns null, the later steps are skipped and the result is null, with no NullPointerException.
A step that itself throws, even a NullPointerException, is not silenced: the same exception reaches the caller.
The function is fixed when it is built: adding a step to the list afterwards changes nothing.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: f.andThen(g) runs f first and then g on its result, which is g(f(x)).
f.compose(g) runs g first and then f on its result, which is f(g(x)).
A step that returns null hands null to the next step, so a chain has to guard against it.
UnaryOperator is a Function from a type to that same type.
